# The Heat Is Urban: How Cities Can Tame Summer's Worst

Summer heat has always been dangerous, but the modern city has made it deadlier. Urban areas run one to seven degrees Fahrenheit hotter than their surrounding countryside—a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect—and in some neighborhoods, the gap is far wider. The reason is straightforward: cities replaced vegetation and soil with asphalt, concrete, and dark rooftops, materials that absorb sunlight all day and release it slowly at night. When a heat wave strikes, as it did in Phoenix in 2023, when temperatures held above 110 degrees for thirty-one consecutive days, or in Chicago in 1995, when more than 700 people died over a single week, the city itself becomes part of the killer. The good news is that this is a design problem, and design problems can be solved. Cities that take heat seriously have a toolkit available: trees, smarter streets, better housing, and robust public transit. The catch is that every tool involves tradeoffs, and residents—not just planners—must live with them.
